title: Spell a Number in English
statement:
Given a non-negative integer num, return how you would write it out in English words, the way it might appear on a cheque.

Use these exact rules so there is one correct answer:

  • Every word starts with a capital letter, and words are separated by single spaces, with no leading or trailing space.
  • No "and" and no hyphens: 342 is "Three Hundred Forty Two".
  • The words are Zero to Nineteen, the tens Twenty to Ninety, and the scale words Hundred, Thousand, Million, Billion.
  • A group that is zero is left out entirely, together with its scale word. Zero is only used for the number 0 itself.

examples.why: The hundreds digit of the last group is 0, so there is no "Zero Hundred". 12 is a teen word, not "Ten Two".
The thousands group is 000, so neither its words nor the word "Thousand" appear.
The only case where "Zero" is said. An implementation that skips empty groups would return an empty string here.

tests.expected: Fifty Thousand Eight Hundred Sixty Eight
Nine Hundred Ninety Nine Thousand Nine Hundred Ninety Nine
Two Billion One Hundred Forty Seven Million Four Hundred Eighty Three Thousand Six Hundred Forty Seven
Five Million Nine Hundred Ninety Nine Thousand Forty

hints: English reads big numbers in groups of three digits. How do you say any number from 1 to 999?
Write a helper for 1–999: hundreds digit plus "Hundred", then either a word under 20 or a tens word plus a ones word. Then split num into groups of three from the right.
Attach Billion, Million, Thousand or nothing to each group, skip groups that are zero, and handle 0 separately at the very start.

explain.intuition:
Every large number is spoken as a list of three-digit groups with a scale word after each: 2 147 483 647 is "two billion, one hundred forty seven million, …". So the whole problem reduces to saying a number from 1 to 999, plus a loop that peels off groups of three with % 1000 and / 1000.

Below 1000, the only irregular part is under 20: eleven to nineteen are their own words. Everything else is mechanical: a hundreds word, a tens word, a ones word. The hard part of this problem is not the algorithm but the edge cases: zero groups, zero digits inside a group, and zero itself.
steps: Write three(n) for 1 ≤ n ≤ 999: if n ≥ 100, emit the hundreds digit's word and "Hundred"; then if the rest is under 20 and not 0, emit its word; otherwise emit the tens word and, if the ones digit is not 0, its word.
Walk the scales Billion, Million, Thousand, and the plain units. For each, take the group Math.floor(num / scale) % 1000.
If the group is non-zero, append three(group) and the scale word (none for units).
Join all words with single spaces.
pitfalls: Emitting "Thousand" for an empty group, as in 1 000 010.
Treating 10–19 as tens plus ones, which gives "Ten Two" instead of "Twelve".
Double spaces or a trailing space from empty parts. Collect words in a list and join once instead of concatenating strings.

solutions.title: Groups of three, iterative
solutions.idea: Peel off groups of three digits from the top scale down, say each with a 1–999 helper, and add its scale word.

solutions.title: Recursive split
solutions.idea: Spell the part above the largest scale that fits, recursively, then the scale word, then the remainder recursively.

followups: Go the other way: parse an English phrase like "Four Hundred Two Thousand Nine" back into a number.
Support British style with "and" ("One Hundred and Five"). Where exactly does "and" go?
